summary: The believer’s union with Christ in his death, resurrection, and ascension, the source of every saving benefit
readingInstruction: Read Romans 6:1-14, Galatians 2:20, and Ephesians 2:4-10. Today is a doctrinal pause on union with Christ. Notice the repeated phrase “with him” and “in Christ,” and how the believer’s past, present, and future are bound to his.
settingTheScene: If we are justified by grace and where sin increased grace abounded all the more, a person might ask: why not keep sinning so that grace may increase? Paul replies with horror, “By no means!” and gives his answer: a believer cannot go on living in sin, because he has been united to Christ in his death and resurrection. Union with Christ is the deepest category of the Christian life. John Calvin said that Christ and all his benefits come to us through union with him.
observation: “Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?” (Romans 6:3).
“We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4).
“For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his” (Romans 6:5).
“We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin” (Romans 6:6).
“So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus” (Romans 6:11).
“I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).
“And raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6).
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8).
doctrinalFocus:
Union with Christ means that every believer is joined to Christ by the Spirit through faith, so that what is true of him becomes true of us. The New Testament expresses this in phrases such as “in Christ,” “with Christ,” and “Christ in you,” which appear well over a hundred times. This is not a mere figure of speech. It is a real, spiritual, and personal bond. Paul uses images: a body and its head, a vine and its branches, a husband and wife, a building and its cornerstone.

Union with Christ is the source of every saving benefit. Justification: we are counted righteous because we are in him. Sanctification: we are changed because we share his death and resurrection life. Adoption: we are sons because we are in the Son. Perseverance: nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus. And glorification: we will be raised as he was raised. It also shows why the gospel is not only forgiveness but a new life. In Romans 6, the believer’s old self was crucified with Christ, and he now walks in newness of life. The old master, sin, has lost its dominion.

Notice the three tenses of union with Christ. We have died with him (past). We now live to God in him (present). We will be raised with him (future). In Ephesians 2, Paul speaks of the future as already done: God “raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places.” Our life is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3).

Christians differ on whether “baptized into Christ” in Romans 6:3 refers primarily to water baptism, or to the Spirit’s baptism that joins us to Christ, which water baptism pictures. Baptists and Presbyterians also differ about who should be baptized and how. All agree that baptism points to the union with Christ in his death and resurrection that is received by faith.
interpretation:
Paul’s question, “Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?” is answered, “By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?” The believer’s relationship to sin has been broken, not because he has become sinless, but because he has died. He now belongs to another.

“Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?” Paul assumes that every Christian knows this. Baptism pictures union: we go under with Christ in death and come up with him in resurrection. The purpose is clear: “that we too might walk in newness of life.” The Christian life is not a self-improvement program. It is a resurrection life.

The logic is expressed in verses 5 to 7: “If we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his.” The “old self,” the person we were in Adam, was crucified with Christ. The result is not perfection, but freedom: we are no longer slaves to sin. “For one who has died has been set free from sin.” And then comes the command, in three steps. First “consider”: “You also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.” Count it true. Then, “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body.” Finally, present yourselves to God. The commands are built on the indicatives. We obey because of who we are in Christ.

Galatians 2:20 is the personal confession: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” Notice the final clause. Paul’s identity is bound up with Christ’s love and self-giving.

Ephesians 2 sets the same truth in a wider frame. We were dead in trespasses, but God, being rich in mercy, made us alive together with Christ, raised us up with him, and seated us with him in the heavenly places. Why? “So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.” And it is all of grace: “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.”
connection: John 15:1-8 is the vine and the branches. Colossians 2:11-13 and 3:1-4 speak of being buried and raised with Christ. 2 Corinthians 5:17 says if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. 1 Corinthians 12:12-13 describes the body of Christ. Ephesians 1:3-14 lists the blessings “in Christ.” Ephesians 5:25-32 speaks of the mystery of Christ and the church. Galatians 3:26-29 says all are one in Christ Jesus. Romans 8:1 says there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. 2 Peter 1:4 speaks of sharing in the divine nature.
application:
Say the word “consider” to yourself today when you are tempted: consider yourself dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.

Read Galatians 2:20 aloud and make it your own confession.

Think about baptism, yours or someone else’s, as a picture of union with Christ.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that in Christ you have died to sin and been raised to new life.
Ask him to help you live in that union.
Tell him where you are tempted to live as if it were not true.
